short.title: 125,000-Year-Old Poisoned Stone Points Found in #Shorts
short.hook: 125,000-year-old stone points found at Uruq Aljelibah lake shore in Saudi Arabia.
script: 125,000-year-old stone points found at Uruq Aljelibah lake shore in Saudi Arabia.
They show traces of poison from Acokanthera schimperi, a tree used historically in Africa and Arabia.
The tools were likely used to hunt hippos, buffalo and ostriches in a once-freshwater lake ecosystem.
Animal bones and stone tools cluster together, suggesting a focused hunting site with complex tool use.
Researchers say the poison may have been applied to tips, but how it was prepared or if it worked remains unclear.
The site may belong to early modern humans, not Neanderthals, though no human remains were found.
Did early humans use poisoned stone points to hunt megafauna, or did they just use them for intimidation?
Tap the link below for the full case file.
short.description:
At a 125,000-year-old site in southern Saudi Arabia known as Uruq Aljelibah, archaeologists found stone tools with traces of poison from Acokanthera schimperi. The tools were likely used to hunt large animals like hippos and buffalo in a former freshwater lake. The close clustering of tools and bones suggests intentional hunting activity. Researchers note the poison's preparation and effectiveness remain uncertain. The site may have been used by early modern humans, though no human remains were discovered. This site adds to evidence of complex tool use in early human societies. Source: Live Science, https://www.livescience.com/archaeology/middle-east/125-000-year-old-poisoned-stone-points-discovered-on-shore-of-ancient-lake-in-saudi-arabia

fact_check: drops the hedge 'may' from 'the site may belong to early modern humans'
claims 'used to hunt hippos, buffalo and ostriches' without article support — article says 'likely exploited for food' and 'hunting large animals', not specific species
states 'poison from Acokanthera schimperi' without hedging — article says 'chemical residues linked with the arrow poison tree (Acokanthera schimperi)', not confirmed as poison

claims 'how it was prepared or if it worked remains unclear' — article says 'we haven't demonstrated exactly how the poison was prepared or whether it was effective' — this is supported, but the narration drops the hedge 'we haven't demonstrated' and uses stronger phrasing
